items.title: A product to maximise
items.question: Find the value of $f$ at its local maximum. Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the product rule, solve $f'(x) = 0$, and classify each root.

byKey.x-value: 2 is where the maximum is. The question asks for the value $f(2)$.
byKey.min-value: 0 is the value at $x = 0$, the local minimum.

explain.text: $f'(x) = 2xe^{-x} - x^2e^{-x} = x(2 - x)e^{-x}$, zero at $x = 0$ and $x = 2$. Around 2 the sign goes $+$ to $-$: a maximum, $f(2) = 4e^{-2} = 0.5413$.

items.title: Classify every stationary point
items.question: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: $x = 0$ is a stationary point of inflection
$x = 0$ is a local maximum, because $f(0) = 0 > f(1)$
options.why: Being higher than the minimum does not make a peak. Just left of 0, $f' < 0$, so $f$ falls into 0.
$f'(0) = 0$ makes it stationary. $f''(0) = 0$ only means the second test is silent.

options.text: The smallest value of $f$ over all $x$ is $-1$

feedback.correct: Minimum at 1, inflection at 0, and $f(1) = -1$ is the lowest value.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the sign of $12x^2(x - 1)$ either side of 0 and of 1.

byKey.c: Just left of 0, $12x^2(x - 1) < 0$, so $f$ is falling into 0. It is not a peak.
byKey.d: Stationary means $f'(0) = 0$, which holds. $f''(0) = 0$ says nothing about that.
byKey.a: Around 1, $f'$ goes from $-$ to $+$: falling, then rising. That is a minimum.
byKey.b: Near 0, $12x^2 > 0$ and $x - 1 < 0$, so $f' < 0$ on both sides: an inflection.
byKey.e: $f \to \infty$ at both ends and the only trough is $f(1) = 3 - 4 = -1$.

explain.text: Near 0, $f' < 0$ on both sides, so 0 is a stationary point of inflection. At 1, $f'$ goes $-$ to $+$ and $f''(1) = 12 > 0$: a minimum, $f(1) = -1$. As $f \to \infty$ at both ends, $-1$ is the smallest value.

items.title: The box, in general
items.prose: A square card of side $L$ has a square of side $x$ cut from each corner. The sides fold up into an open box of volume $V(x) = x(L - 2x)^2$, for $0 \le x \le \tfrac{L}{2}$.
items.question: Find the cut $x$ that maximises the volume, in terms of $L$.

widget.label: Best cut in terms of L

feedback.correct: $x = \tfrac{L}{6}$: with $L = 30$ that is the 5 cm cut from the lesson.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Factorise $V'(x)$ and keep the root that gives a real box.

byKey.flat: At $x = \tfrac{L}{2}$ the base has no width, so the volume is 0. That root is the minimum.
byKey.quarter: $\tfrac{L}{4}$ is the fence answer. Here $V'(x) = (L - 2x)(L - 6x)$, which is 0 at $\tfrac{L}{6}$.

explain.text: $V'(x) = (L - 2x)^2 - 4x(L - 2x) = (L - 2x)(L - 6x)$, zero at $\tfrac{L}{6}$ and $\tfrac{L}{2}$. $V$ is 0 at both ends and positive between, so $x = \tfrac{L}{6}$ is the maximum, with $V = \tfrac{2L^3}{27}$.

items.title: Derive the Kelly fraction
items.prose: A bet pays $b$ to 1 and wins with probability $p$, with $q = 1 - p$. Staking a fraction $f$ gives growth $G(f) = p\ln(1 + bf) + q\ln(1 - f)$ per bet.
items.question: Put the lines of the derivation of the Kelly fraction in order.

lines.text: $G(f) = p\ln(1 + bf) + q\ln(1 - f)$: the growth per bet
$G'(f) = \dfrac{pb}{1 + bf} - \dfrac{q}{1 - f}$: the chain rule on each log
$pb(1 - f) = q(1 + bf)$: set $G'(f) = 0$ and multiply by $(1 + bf)(1 - f)$
$pb - q = bf(p + q) = bf$: expand, collect $f$, and use $p + q = 1$

feedback.correct: Differentiate, set to 0, clear fractions, collect, divide.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Differentiate first, then solve $G'(f) = 0$ step by step.

byKey.k4: Collecting $f$ comes after clearing the fractions.
byKey.k5: The formula is the last line.

explain.text: Each step is reversible for $0 \le f < 1$, since the factor $(1 + bf)(1 - f)$ is positive. $G''(f) < 0$, so this stationary point is the maximum.

items.prose: A 3-year bond pays a 6% annual coupon on £100 face value. Its yield is 6%, so its price is £100: $P(y) = \dfrac{6}{1+y} + \dfrac{6}{(1+y)^2} + \dfrac{106}{(1+y)^3}$.
items.question: Find its modified duration $D = -\dfrac{P'(y)}{P(y)}$ at $y = 0.06$. Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Differentiate each term with the chain rule, add them at $y = 0.06$, then divide by 100.

byKey.macaulay: 2.833 years is the Macaulay duration. Divide by $1 + y = 1.06$ for the modified duration.
byKey.slope: That is $-P'(0.06)$. Divide it by the price, £100.

items.title: Correcting for convexity
items.question: Estimate $P(0.08)$ with $P + P'\,\Delta y + \tfrac{1}{2}P''(\Delta y)^2$. Give it to the penny.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With $\Delta y = 0.03$: add $-12.63$ and $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 2341.29 \times 0.0009$.

byKey.linear: £83.04 is the tangent alone. Add the convexity term $\tfrac{1}{2}P''(\Delta y)^2 = 1.05$.
byKey.no-half: You left out the $\tfrac{1}{2}$ in the convexity term. It is $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 2341.29 \times 0.0009 = 1.05$.

explain.text: $95.67 - 12.63 + \tfrac{1}{2}(2341.29)(0.0009) = 95.67 - 12.63 + 1.05 = 84.09$. The tangent alone was 99p out; the convexity term cuts the error to 6p.

items.title: Three rounds
items.prose: Apply L’Hôpital’s rule as many times as it takes.
items.question: Find $\lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{x - \sin x}{x^3}$. Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The form stays $\tfrac{0}{0}$ for two rounds; apply the rule three times.

byKey.stop-early: You read a $\tfrac{0}{0}$ along the way as 0. Keep applying the rule until the form is not $\tfrac{0}{0}$.
byKey.third: You lost the factor from differentiating $3x^2$: it gives $6x$, not $3x$.

explain.text: Three rounds: $\tfrac{1 - \cos x}{3x^2}$, then $\tfrac{\sin x}{6x}$, then $\tfrac{\cos x}{6} \to \tfrac{1}{6}$. So near 0, $\sin x \approx x - \tfrac{x^3}{6}$.

items.title: A product in disguise
items.prose: As $x \to 0^+$, $x \to 0$ while $\ln x \to -\infty$. Rewrite $x\ln x = \dfrac{\ln x}{1/x}$.
items.question: What is $\lim_{x \to 0^+} x\ln x$?

options.why: $x$ shrinks to 0 faster than $\ln x$ grows. The rule shows it: $\tfrac{1/x}{-1/x^2} = -x \to 0$.
A product of something going to 0 and something going to $-\infty$ has no automatic value. The rule gives 0.
It exists. As $\tfrac{\ln x}{1/x}$ the form is $\tfrac{\infty}{\infty}$, and the rule settles it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply the rule to $\dfrac{\ln x}{1/x}$.

explain.text: $\tfrac{\ln x}{1/x}$ has the form $\tfrac{-\infty}{\infty}$. The rule gives $\tfrac{1/x}{-1/x^2} = -x \to 0$. At $x = 0.001$, $x\ln x = -0.0069$.

items.title: The Kelly bet, start to finish
items.prompt:
A bet pays $b$ to 1 and wins with probability $p$, with $q = 1 - p$. You stake a fraction $f$ of your bankroll on each bet, $0 \le f < 1$. The long-run growth rate per bet is $G(f) = p\ln(1 + bf) + q\ln(1 - f)$.

(a) Find $G'(f)$ and solve $G'(f) = 0$, justifying each step.

(b) Show that the stationary point is a maximum.

(c) Take $p = 0.55$ and $b = 1$. Find $f^*$ and $G(f^*)$.

(d) For the same bet, find $G(0.2)$, twice the Kelly stake, and say what it means.

(e) What should you stake if $p - \tfrac{q}{b} \le 0$? Justify using the interval $0 \le f < 1$.
items.model:
**(a)** By the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{df}\ln(1 + bf) = \dfrac{b}{1 + bf}$ and $\dfrac{d}{df}\ln(1 - f) = \dfrac{-1}{1 - f}$. So
$$G'(f) = \frac{pb}{1 + bf} - \frac{q}{1 - f}.$$
Set $G'(f) = 0$ and multiply by $(1 + bf)(1 - f)$, which is positive for $0 \le f < 1$:
$$pb(1 - f) = q(1 + bf).$$
Expand: $pb - pbf = q + qbf$. Collect the $f$ terms: $pb - q = bf(p + q) = bf$, since $p + q = 1$. Divide by $b > 0$:
$$f^* = \frac{pb - q}{b} = p - \frac{q}{b}.$$

**(b)** Differentiate again:
$$G''(f) = -\frac{pb^2}{(1 + bf)^2} - \frac{q}{(1 - f)^2}.$$
Both terms are negative for every $f$ in $0 \le f < 1$, so $G'' < 0$. Hence $G'$ is decreasing, $G'$ changes from $+$ to $-$ at $f^*$, and $f^*$ is a maximum (the only stationary point).

**(c)** With $p = 0.55$, $q = 0.45$, $b = 1$: $f^* = 0.55 - 0.45 = 0.1$. Then
$$G(0.1) = 0.55\ln 1.1 + 0.45\ln 0.9 = 0.55(0.09531) + 0.45(-0.10536) = 0.05242 - 0.04741 \approx 0.0050.$$
About 0.5% log growth per bet: over 1,000 bets the bankroll grows by a factor of about $e^{5.0} \approx 150$.

**(d)** $G(0.2) = 0.55\ln 1.2 + 0.45\ln 0.8 = 0.55(0.18232) + 0.45(-0.22314) = 0.10028 - 0.10041 \approx -0.00014.$
At twice the Kelly stake the growth rate is slightly negative: in the long run the bankroll shrinks, even though every bet has a positive expected profit. Near its peak $G$ is close to a symmetric cap, and $G(0) = 0$, so $G(2f^*) \approx 0$. Over-betting is far more costly than under-betting.

**(e)** $G'(0) = pb - q$. If $p - \tfrac{q}{b} \le 0$ then $pb - q \le 0$, so $G'(0) \le 0$. Since $G'$ is decreasing (part (b)), $G'(f) < 0$ for every $f > 0$, and $G$ falls across $0 \le f < 1$. The largest value on the interval is at the end $f = 0$: do not bet.

rubric.text: Differentiates both logs with the chain rule: $G'(f) = \tfrac{pb}{1 + bf} - \tfrac{q}{1 - f}$.
Solves $G'(f) = 0$ to $f^* = p - \tfrac{q}{b}$, noting the positive factor cleared and using $p + q = 1$.
Finds $G''(f) < 0$ on the interval and concludes the stationary point is a maximum.
Gets $G(0.2) \approx -0.00014$ and explains that twice Kelly gives no long-run growth despite a positive edge.
Shows $G$ is decreasing when $pb - q \le 0$, so the best stake is the end $f = 0$.
